article.title: Authoritarians Fear Education
article.author: Peter McLaren
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Kural is an Indian progressive digital platform and publication that recently published a comprehensive, three-part interview with Peter McLaren, a renowned Canadian-American scholar and a leading architect of critical pedagogy. Conducted by doctoral researcher Naila Alavi, the feature interview—headlined "Who Gets to Imagine the Future?"—delves into the current state of education and social theory. Foreword Naila Alavi I first encountered Peter McLaren in the first semester of my master’s, not in person, of course, but in the way one first encounters many of the people who eventually become important to one’s intellectual life. I met him on a reading list. At the time, I was beginning to think more seriously about classrooms and the politics that inhabit them. Over the years, as my own questions moved towards education, childhood, emotion, and the ways in which institutions participate in shaping how we understand ourselves and the worlds around us, I kept finding my way back to critical pedagogy and Peter’s work. Some scholars give you answers. Others alter the questions you know how to ask. My relationship with Peter’s scholarship has been closer to the latter. Years later, The Kural brought those questions into an entirely different kind of space. The Kural began with a group of us wanting to make something together. We had spent years inside universities, writing papers, dissertations, assignments, and research that often travelled only as far as another classroom, another evaluator, or another academic conversation. We began wondering what might happen if some of that thinking were allowed another life. We wanted a space in which research could be reworked without being emptied of its complexity, where people could write seriously without always having to write academically, and where a photograph, an interview, an essay, a keyword, or an unfinished reflection could all become ways of thinking in public. There was no grand institution behind us when we began. The Kural was, and remains, something built collectively by people who believed there was value in creating such a space and were willing to do the often-invisible work required to sustain it. We have argued over words and layouts, returned drafts to one another, worried about accessibility and rigour, thought about whose voices we were making room for, and repeatedly asked ourselves what it means to take an idea produced somewhere and help it reach somewhere else. Somewhere along the way, a phrase became important to how we understood what we were trying to do. “We wanted to make thought travel”. An interview with Peter McLaren emerged naturally from those conversations. When we began thinking about whom The Kural should speak with, we wanted a conversation that would speak to the questions from which the platform itself had emerged. What happens to critical thought when the spaces that sustain it come under pressure? Why do classrooms, universities, books, curricula, histories, and even particular words become objects of such intense political struggle? What exactly is at stake when power becomes invested in determining not only what people know, but what they remember, what they fear, and what they are permitted to imagine? Peter seemed, to us, an especially important person with whom to think through these questions. I began the interview with education. I thought we were going to talk about classrooms, universities, curricula, and the contemporary assault on academic spaces. We did. But Peter kept taking the conversation somewhere larger. A question about why power fears classrooms became a conversation about memory and historical agency. A question about children opened onto the political struggle over who is permitted to shape the future. When we moved to the language of humiliation, resentment, national injury, and moral panic, Peter brought political economy into conversation with affect and showed how structures of domination must also acquire an emotional life. From there, the conversation moved through attention and distraction, through imagination and the possibility of alternatives, until we eventually arrived at algorithms, digital infrastructures, surveillance, affective publics, and what he describes as post-digital fascism. Reading his responses as they arrived, I began to realize that the conversation had acquired a movement of its own. This is why we eventually published it in three parts in The Kural . The sections followed that movement. We began with the politics of education and the question of who gets to imagine the future. We then moved into the politics of feeling, attention, and imagination. Finally, we arrived at a question that seemed to gather much of what had preceded it. Where does critical pedagogy live now? Peter’s answer to that final question is something I often return to. The classroom, he tells us, remains important, but critical pedagogy cannot remain there. It has to find life in reading groups and community organizations, in independent media and digital commons, in cultural movements, artistic collaborations, and the many other places where people come together to learn, question, remember, and imagine. He reminds us that learning to read the world critically today also means learning to read the algorithms, platforms, and infrastructures through which so much of that world now reaches us. There was something moving about arriving there because, on a vastly smaller scale, it brought us back to the impulse with which The Kural had begun. We, too, had been wondering where thought lives once it leaves the classroom. We too wanted to believe that serious intellectual work could have a public life, that thinking could happen across forms and outside established academic spaces, and that making room for such conversations was itself worthwhile. There is another reason this conversation means a great deal to us. The Kural was new. We were still learning how to become the thing we had imagined. Peter could very easily have treated an invitation from a young, independent platform as one more request in an already crowded academic life. Instead, he gave us his time. More than that, he gave the questions his attention. His responses were long, patient, generous, and serious. He never made us feel that the size of the platform determined the seriousness with which its questions deserved to be received. For that, The Kural is deeply grateful to Peter McLaren. We are grateful not only for the interview he gave us, but for the trust with which he allowed a young platform to carry his words. We are grateful for the generosity with which he stayed with our questions and for the expansiveness with which he answered them. And I am personally grateful for the strange and lovely distance travelled between encountering Peter McLaren as a name on a reading list and finding myself, years later, asking him some of the questions that his own scholarship had helped me learn how to ask. The conversation was first given a home by The Kural . Its appearance in LA Progressive now gives it another life and another readership. I find something fitting in that. A conversation about the places in which critical thought can live has itself refused to remain in one place. When we began The Kural , we wanted to make thought travel. Peter helped us do precisely that. And now, very generously, he is helping it travel further. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship Part I - Who Gets to Imagine the Future? PART ONE WHO GETS TO IMAGINE THE FUTURE ? 1. Across the world, authoritarian politics increasingly begins its cultural project by attacking universities, rewriting textbooks, banning words, policing teachers, and dismantling spaces where people gather to think critically. Why does power fear classrooms so deeply? What is it about collective thinking itself that becomes dangerous to right-wing projects? McLaren: When my name appeared on Professor Watchlist, a project created by Turning Point USA under the leadership of the recently assassinated Charlie Kirk, I was reminded of a lesson that authoritarian movements have understood for centuries: if you want to control a society, you must first shape how it remembers, how it thinks, and how it learns. Kirk was one of the most influential figures within the contemporary American right, a close ally of Donald Trump, and a leading advocate of a form of Christian nationalism that sought to fuse religious identity with an increasingly authoritarian political vision. His organization devoted considerable energy to targeting educators, students, and academic institutions deemed insufficiently loyal to conservative values. The purpose of Professor Watchlist was ostensibly to expose professors accused of promoting “radical” ideas. In reality, it functioned as part of a broader campaign to intimidate critical educators and portray intellectual inquiry itself as a threat. I was hardly alone. Hundreds of professors found themselves publicly targeted. Yet the existence of such a project raises an important question: if classrooms are politically insignificant, why devote so much effort to policing them? What authoritarian movements fear is not simply knowledge but the possibility that ordinary people might come to recognize themselves as makers of history rather than objects of history. The contemporary attack on universities, teachers, libraries, curricula, and public intellectuals is not accidental. Throughout history, authoritarian movements have understood something that liberal democracies often forget: education is never merely about the transmission of knowledge. It is fundamentally a struggle over consciousness itself. Power fears classrooms because classrooms contain the possibility that people might begin to read the world critically rather than simply adapt to it. Authoritarian projects depend upon naturalizing existing social arrangements. They seek to convince people that hierarchy is inevitable, that inequality is deserved, that nationalism is synonymous with patriotism, and that the present order represents the only realistic future. Critical education disrupts these assumptions. It opens spaces where students can ask dangerous questions: Who benefits from existing arrangements? Whose voices have been excluded from history? Why do certain forms of suffering persist? What alternatives might be possible? The issue is not simply knowledge but collective knowledge. A solitary individual may question authority in private, but when people gather to analyze their experiences, compare their histories, and imagine alternatives, criticism can become a social force. Authoritarian movements recognize that classrooms, universities, and cultural institutions can function as laboratories of democratic possibility. They are among the few public spaces where people learn to connect personal troubles with larger structures of power and to recognize themselves as historical agents rather than passive spectators. This is why attacks on education are so often accompanied by efforts to rewrite textbooks, ban books, police language, censor teachers, and manufacture historical amnesia. Whether in the United States, India, Brazil, Hungary, Turkey, or elsewhere, the pattern is remarkably familiar. The path toward authoritarian rule is frequently paved by efforts to subordinate education to nationalist mythology, cultural conformity, and ideological loyalty. Such measures are designed not merely to suppress information but to regulate memory itself. Memory is dangerous because it reminds us that societies have changed before and therefore can change again. Historical consciousness undermines the authoritarian fantasy that the existing order is permanent, natural, or sacred. What right-wing authoritarian projects fear most is not disagreement but the emergence of democratic publics capable of critical reflection. They fear forms of collective thinking that expose the contradictions of power, reveal the humanity of those who have been marginalized, and cultivate the capacity to imagine a world different from the one we have inherited. At its best, education teaches people that reality is not a fate to which we must submit but a field of struggle in which we can intervene. The deepest threat that critical education poses to authoritarianism is that it transforms people from objects of history into subjects of history. It teaches them that the world they inhabit was made by human beings and can therefore be remade by human beings. Every authoritarian project seeks to close the future by declaring that there is no alternative. Every critical classroom reopens the future by reminding us that history remains unfinished. For this reason, the classroom remains one of the most important political spaces in society. It is one of the few places where critical dialogue can challenge manufactured ignorance, where hope can confront cynicism, and where people can learn that democracy is not merely a method of governance but a way of living together. Authoritarianism begins by attacking the institutions that teach people how to think. Critical pedagogy begins by helping people discover that the future is still theirs to create. Related: Che Guevara, Paulo Freire, Cuba, and the Future of Hope PART TWO Part 2: The Politics of Feeling, Attention, and Imagination You have written extensively about capitalism's influence on education. Yet many contemporary struggles over universities and curricula seem to be framed less through economic arguments than through narratives of humiliation, cultural decline, national injury, moral corruption, or the feeling that a way of life is under threat. How do you understand the relationship between these emotional narratives and broader structures of political and economic power? To what extent do projects of domination operate through the management of collective emotions as much as through material conditions? McLaren: For many years, I have argued that capitalism exerts a profound influence on education, shaping not only what schools teach but also how societies define knowledge, success, citizenship, and human worth. Yet it would be a mistake to assume that systems of domination operate primarily through economic mechanisms alone. Political and economic power must also work through culture, identity, memory, and emotion. Human beings do not live by material interests alone. We live through stories, fears, aspirations, resentments, and hopes. This is one reason why contemporary authoritarian movements often speak less about economics than about humiliation, decline, national injury, moral corruption, or the loss of a cherished way of life. Such narratives perform important political work. They translate complex structural problems into emotionally compelling stories that identify enemies, assign blame, and promise redemption. Periods of economic insecurity, growing inequality, precarious employment, ecological crisis, and social fragmentation create widespread anxiety. Yet the causes of these conditions are often difficult to identify and even more difficult to challenge. Rather than directing attention toward structural inequalities, concentrations of wealth, or the contradictions of capitalism itself, authoritarian movements frequently redirect these anxieties toward symbolic targets. Intellectuals, immigrants, racial minorities, journalists, teachers, feminists, LGBTQ communities, and political dissidents become convenient objects onto which social frustrations can be projected. In this sense, emotional narratives do not replace political economy; they mediate it. They transform economic contradictions into cultural grievances. They convert structural insecurity into moral panic. They encourage people to experience systemic problems as the consequence of betrayal by internal enemies rather than as the result of unequal social relations. What concerns me most is that these narratives often operate through the politics of dispossession. People are encouraged to believe that something essential has been stolen from them: their nation, their culture, their traditions, their status, their faith, or their future. The language of loss becomes politically powerful because it speaks to genuine experiences of uncertainty and dislocation. But instead of offering democratic solutions, authoritarian movements channel these feelings toward exclusionary and often punitive forms of politics. The educational sphere becomes particularly important in this process because education shapes how people interpret their experiences. Schools, universities, libraries, and cultural institutions help determine whether citizens understand social problems historically and critically or through myths of national innocence and civilizational decline. This helps explain why educational institutions have become such prominent targets across the globe. The struggle is not merely over curriculum. It is a struggle over collective memory and public consciousness. Authoritarian movements understand that if people learn to examine history critically, to recognize structures of power, and to imagine alternatives to existing arrangements, then the emotional foundations of authoritarian politics begin to weaken. This is where concepts such as epistemicide and scholasticide become particularly important. Epistemicide refers to the destruction or erasure of entire ways of knowing. Scholasticide refers to the destruction of educational institutions, intellectual life, and the social conditions necessary for learning itself. Both involve more than attacks on knowledge. They are attacks on the collective capacity to imagine different futures. They seek to narrow the horizons of thought and feeling, making existing relations of power appear natural, inevitable, and beyond challenge. Paulo Freire understood that domination requires more than economic exploitation. It also requires shaping consciousness. People must be persuaded that the world cannot be otherwise. They must be encouraged to internalize limits on what they believe is possible. This is why critical pedagogy places such emphasis on conscientização, or critical consciousness. The struggle for liberation is not only a struggle over material conditions. It is also a struggle over perception, meaning, and hope. What we are witnessing today is therefore not simply a conflict between competing political programs. It is a contest over public feeling itself. Authoritarian movements seek to organize fear, resentment, nostalgia, humiliation, and grievance into political forces capable of sustaining existing hierarchies. Democratic movements, by contrast, must cultivate different emotional capacities: solidarity, compassion, critical reflection, historical memory, and hope. Hope, in this sense, is not a sentiment. It is a political force. It is the refusal to accept that the future has already been decided. Authoritarian projects thrive when people become convinced that alternatives are impossible. Democratic education begins from the opposite assumption: that history remains open, that human beings possess the capacity to transform the conditions they inherit, and that another world remains possible. For this reason, the struggle over education is inseparable from the struggle over collective emotions. Whoever shapes how people feel about the past, the present, and the future exercises enormous influence over political life itself. The battle is not only over institutions or resources. It is also over fear and hope, memory and imagination, despair and possibility. Ultimately, it is a struggle over how people understand themselves as historical agents capable of shaping the world they inhabit. Related: Revolutionary Prophetic Pedagogy: Reclaiming Schools for Democracy in an Age of Oligarchy Part III - Where Does Critical Pedagogy Live Now? WHERE DOES CRITICAL PEDAGOGY LIVE NOW? 1. Critical pedagogy has long imagined the classroom as a space of emancipation. But many young people today encounter politics primarily through algorithms, short-form outrage, influencer culture, and digital propaganda rather than classrooms. In such a world, where does critical pedagogy live now? Can the classroom still compete with the emotional machinery of the internet? McLaren: Critical pedagogy has traditionally imagined the classroom as a space where students learn to question assumptions, interrogate power, and develop the critical capacities necessary for democratic citizenship. But we must recognize that the educational terrain has changed dramatically. Today, many young people encounter politics less through classrooms than through algorithms, influencers, social media feeds, digital spectacles, and what I have elsewhere called the emerging culture of post-digital fascism. The crucial question is therefore not whether the classroom can compete with the internet. The question is whether critical pedagogy can expand beyond the classroom and confront the new pedagogical forces shaping consciousness in the digital age. One of the central mistakes made by many educators is to assume that platforms such as TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, X, and other social media ecosystems are merely technologies of communication. They are not. They are pedagogical machines. They teach continuously. They teach values, identities, desires, fears, habits of attention, and modes of political engagement. They shape how people understand themselves and the world. The contemporary digital landscape functions as an enormous educational apparatus operating largely outside democratic accountability. Algorithms decide what receives visibility and what disappears into obscurity. Outrage is rewarded. Nuance is penalized. Emotional intensity travels farther than careful reasoning. The result is a culture increasingly organized around spectacle, speed, and affect. This is one reason I have written about post-digital fascism. Unlike the authoritarian movements of the twentieth century, contemporary forms of domination operate through sophisticated digital infrastructures that shape consciousness long before explicit political messages appear. Power increasingly works through algorithms, data extraction, surveillance technologies, influencer cultures, affective manipulation, and attention economies that reward grievance, resentment, and polarization. The danger is not simply misinformation. The danger is the transformation of subjectivity itself. Digital technologies increasingly function as what I have called factories of affect. They organize emotions before they organize ideas. They shape how people feel before they shape what people think. Fear, outrage, humiliation, resentment, and anxiety circulate through networks at extraordinary speed, generating what might be called affective publics—communities held together less by shared analysis than by shared emotional intensities. Authoritarian movements understand this terrain remarkably well. They communicate not primarily through rational argument but through spectacle. They mobilize identities, fears, and fantasies. They create digital ecosystems in which grievance becomes a source of belonging and outrage becomes a form of political participation. The far right often understands the emotional architecture of digital culture far better than liberal institutions that continue to believe politics is primarily a matter of policy debate. The challenge for critical pedagogy is therefore immense. Yet I do not believe it is hopeless. The classroom remains important, but it can no longer be understood as the exclusive site of critical education. Critical pedagogy must become a broader democratic project operating across cultural, political, and digital spaces. It must help students understand not only texts but platforms, not only ideologies but algorithms, not only institutions but infrastructures of perception. Students today need forms of critical literacy capable of revealing how digital systems shape attention, manufacture desire, monetize outrage, and normalize particular visions of reality. They need to understand how surveillance capitalism transforms human experience into data and how algorithmic systems increasingly influence what societies remember, forget, fear, and desire. At the same time, critical pedagogy must offer alternatives. It cannot survive as a language of critique alone. It must help create what might be called alternative cognitive ecologies—spaces where dialogue, reflection, solidarity, and democratic imagination can flourish outside the imperatives of digital extraction and commodification. This may take the form of reading groups, community organizations, independent media projects, digital commons, cultural movements, artistic collaborations, and new forms of democratic association. The goal is not to retreat from technology but to democratize our relationship to it. Paulo Freire taught us that education is fundamentally about learning to read the world critically. Today, the world increasingly arrives through screens. To read the world critically now requires reading algorithms, platforms, data systems, and digital infrastructures as carefully as previous generations learned to read newspapers, governments, and institutions. The struggle before us is therefore not merely educational. It is civilizational. The question is whether digital technologies will continue to function as instruments of surveillance, commodification, distraction, and authoritarian manipulation, or whether they can become part of a democratic project grounded in dialogue, solidarity, justice, and collective flourishing. I remain hopeful because authoritarianism ultimately depends upon closing down human possibility. Critical pedagogy begins from the opposite premise. It insists that human beings are unfinished, that history remains open, and that new futures can still be created. The classroom alone cannot compete with the emotional machinery of the internet. But critical pedagogy was never meant to remain confined to classrooms. It lives wherever people gather to question, to learn, to imagine, to remember, and to struggle collectively for a more democratic world. In the age of post-digital fascism, that mission becomes more urgent than ever. Naila Alavi is a final-year undergraduate student from Aligarh Muslim University. Due to her general skepticism concerning society, she has been drawn to the study of gender issues and minority rights.
